articles.title: Padres closer Mason Miller added to paternity list, will miss pivotal Game 3 on Tuesday vs. Brewers
articles.summary: Miller was tied for third in MLB in saves this year with 38.
articles.body:
The San Diego Padres are one game away from elimination, down 2-0 to the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. They'll be without their All-Star closer as they try to extend their season.

MLB approved a roster change for San Diego, as closer Mason Miller is going on the postseason paternity list and will not be available for Game 3 on Tuesday .

The Padres replaced Miller with reliever Wandy Peralta.

The MLB playoffs come with specific roster rules. A team must submit a roster for each series. If a player is replaced during a series due to injury, he must miss that series and , if the team advances, the following series.

But Miller was added to the postseason paternity list, and there are different rules for that. He can miss a minimum of one day and a maximum of three. When he returns, he can replace Peralta without being forced to sit out another series if San Diego makes a comeback against Milwaukee.

Miller is one of baseball's best closers. He had a career-high 38 saves this season in 66 appearances and finished with a 1.67 ERA.

The 35-year-old Peralta gives the Padres an extra lefty out of the bullpen. He made 65 appearances this season and went 3-3 with a 3.61 ERA.

San Diego heads into Tuesday's Game 3 on the brink of elimination in the best-of-five series. Games 1 and 2 both came down to the wire, with the Brew Crew winning each by one run.

Miller blew the save in Game 2 , when Jackson Chourio laced a walk-off single to center that drove in both Sal Frelick and Christian Yelich, giving Milwaukee a 4-3 victory.

If the Padres lose without Miller on Tuesday, their season is over. If San Diego wins at home Tuesday, the series will continue with Game 4 on Wednesday in San Diego, and Miller would be eligible to return.

articles.title: Dodgers-Braves: Freddie Freeman was booed and robbed of a home run in his return to Atlanta. He got revenge in his next at-bat
articles.summary: Freddie Freeman delivered countless clutch moments for the home team in 12 seasons with the Atlanta Braves. On Tuesday, he delivered one for the visitors.
articles.body:
Freddie Freeman delivered countless clutch moments in the five seasons he played at Truist Park with the Atlanta Braves.

On Tuesday, he delivered one for the visitors after being greeted with boos and being robbed of a home run in Game 3 of the National League Division Series .

With his Los Angeles Dodgers holding a 2-0 lead thanks to a Kiké Hernández home run in the fourth inning, Freeman followed with one of his own two batters later.

With the bases clear and two outs in frame, Braves starter Chris Sale threw a sinker down and inside. Freeman turned on it and sent it clear over the right-field wall.

The solo shot extended the Dodgers' lead to 3-0 and and provided redemption for Freeman after he was robbed of a home run just one inning earlier.

With a man on and no outs in the third, Freeman hit a deep shot off Sale that appeared destined to clear the short fence in left field.

But Mauricio Dubón had a bead on the ball off the bat from his position in left. He leapt in front of the Dodgers' bullpen and corralled the ball before it cleared the fence.

Replay shows that the ball was almost certainly going over the fence had Dubón not gotten there to make the play.

That home-run robbery came on the heels of Freeman being greeted with boos from the Atlanta crowd, who went on to cheer his first-inning strikeout.

But Freeman is a former MVP and three-time World Series champion for a reason. He wasn't fazed by the moment or the hostile Atlanta crowd on Tuesday.

Freeman won his MVP and his first World Series title with the Braves during his 12 seasons with the franchise. Tuesday marked his first playoff game in Atlanta since he left to sign with the Dodgers, whom he has since helped lead to two World Series championships.

There will surely be a chance for Braves fans to celebrate Freeman again after he's retired. But for now, there's no love lost with a trip to the NLCS on the line.

And there's no backing down from Freeman.

articles.title: Dodgers push Braves to the brink of MLB playoff exit
articles.summary: Enrique Hernandez and Freddie Freeman smacked home runs Tuesday to power the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers over Atlanta 3-1 and to the brink of adva...
articles.body:
Enrique Hernandez and Freddie Freeman smacked home runs Tuesday to power the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers over Atlanta 3-1 and to the brink of advancing in the Major League Baseball playoffs.

A two-run blast by Hernandez and a solo shot by former Braves star Freeman in the fourth inning combined with a stellar pitching effort from Japan's Yoshinobu Yamamoto to seal Atlanta's fate.

Yamamoto, a 28-year-old right-hander, struck out 10, matching his MLB career high, while surrendering only one run on four hits over seven innings.

"I was feeling really good. I was able to control my pitches," said Yamamoto through a translator. "That's why I got the swings and misses.

"My fastball was coming out of my hand pretty good so naturally I ended up relying on it."

The Dodgers took a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five National League divisional series, which continues in Atlanta on Wednesday.

The reigning World Series champion Dodgers are trying to win a third consecutive title, something no NL club has ever done.

In a later game, the Milwaukee Brewers seek a road victory at San Diego to complete a sweep of the Padres and reach the best-of-seven NL Championship Series (NLCS) for the second consecutive year.

The Dodgers swept Milwaukee in last year's NLCS.

Yamamoto, last year's World Series Most Valuable Player, improved to 8-1 in his MLB playoff career.

Atlanta ace Chris Sale started against Yamamoto. It was only the third game in MLB playoff history, the first since 1938, with rival starters who both had closed out a World Series-clinching contest.

Sale, a 37-year-old left-hander who threw his first shutout since 2019 in August against the Dodgers, struck out seven while allowing three runs on seven hits over five innings.

After Andy Pages singled to open the fourth, Hernandez smashed a two-run homer over the left-field wall to open the scoring.

Freeman, robbed of a homer by Mauricio Dubon's leaping catch in the third inning, followed moments later with a solo homer for a 3-0 Los Angeles lead.

That gave the Dodgers their first 10 runs of the playoffs all from homers, the longest such streak to start a post-season in MLB history.

Dubon and Lane Thomas opened the Atlanta fifth with back-to-back singles and Yamamoto walked Rowdy Tellez to load the bases.

Drake Baldwin grounded out to first to drive in Dubon from third base but Ronald Acuna grounded out to end the threat.

The Braves threatened in the ninth inning after Ozzie Albies doubled off reliever Edwin Diaz and took third on a Michael Harris ground out.

Dubon then hit a fly out and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to end the game.

Dodgers designated hitter Shohei Ohtani, a four-time MVP who has battled right biceps and left knee injuries, was dropped to fifth in the batting order, his lowest spot in six years.

The Japanese star went 0-for-2 with a walk and a strikeout.

articles.title: Dodgers hit two homers off Chris Sale to steal game three of NLDS behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto
articles.summary: Dave Roberts made a gutsy call turning to Edwin Diaz for the final three outs as the Los Angeles Dodgers clung to a Game 3 lead over Atlanta.
articles.body: The division series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Atlanta Braves pitted two very good, division-winning teams against each other. And through three games, it's been the tight, hard-fought contest you'd expect given the impressive collection of talent on both teams. While the Dodgers jumped out to a 5-1 lead thanks to home runs from Teoscar Hernandez, Kyle Tucker, and Max Muncy, the Braves battled back in the 9th inning with a two-run homer of their own from Ozzie Albies. It was a sign of things to come in the ensuing games. Game two seemed to set up perfectly for Los Angeles to take command of the series. Instead of using Chris Sale, the Braves decided to give their superstar starter another few days of rest, as they did for much of the regular season. Instead of Chris Sale, the Braves went for a bullpen game, opened by Ray Kerr. WHITE SOX RIDE ANOTHER DRAMATIC COMEBACK WIN TO BEAT GUARDIANS AND TAKE COMMANDING 2-0 ALDS LEAD Two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell, going up against the Braves bullpen and Ray Kerr. But as is so often the case in Major League Baseball, particularly postseason baseball, it didn't work out that way. Kerr was excellent, and reliever Didier Fuentes was even better, going 3.2 innings with just one run allowed. Snell didn't have it, walking five hitters, though limited the damage to just one run himself. Atlanta pushed across two runs, one coming on a series of uncharacteristic Dodger misplays. Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez misplayed a fly ball to left field, turning an out into a triple for Michael Harris II. Harris then immediately scored on a wild pitch from reliever Kris Bubic, before doubling in the third run of the game in the 7th inning. Max Muncy homered with the Dodgers down to their last strike to make it 3-2, but Josue De Paula popped up to end it and even the series at a game apiece. That set up a pivotal game three in Atlanta, with Sale now available on regular rest, going against World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Exactly what postseason baseball should be. Sale, who'd obliterated the Dodgers in August, allowing just five hits and striking out 11 in a complete game shutout, looked to be the overwhelming favorite to take down the Dodgers' struggling lefties. Including Shohei Ohtani, who's been far from himself after a number of mid-season injuries. But Yamamoto is pretty exceptional himself, a fact both starters acknowledged in a fantastic pregame tribute from one star to another. Surprisingly though, Sale didn't have his best stuff. Two first inning baserunners and long counts ran his pitch count up, and only the Dodgers' prolific incompetence with runners in scoring position prevented the score from spiraling out of control. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE With Yamamoto cruising, the Dodgers once again had an opportunity to take control of the game in the third inning. With Mookie Betts on first, Freddie Freeman hit a deep fly ball to left field that looked like it was headed over the wall...until Mauricio Dubon made a spectacular play to bring it back. In the fourth though, the Dodgers finally broke through. The struggling Andy Pages singled off Sale to lead off the inning, before Kyle Tucker struck out. That brought postseason hero Kike Hernandez to the plate, starting his first game of the postseason. And Hernandez struck again in October, crushing a low change up into the left field seats for a 2-0 lead. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! A few hitters later, Freeman came up and hit another bomb, this time well out of Dubon's reach. Yamamoto kept dealing until the bottom of the 5th, when the Braves mounted a rally behind singles from Dubon and Lane Thomas. Rowdy Tellez walked in a bout of unusual wildness from the Dodgers starter, loading the bases for the top of the Atlanta lineup. STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW! Drake Baldwin grounded out to first to bring in a run, but Yamamoto bore down and got Ronald Acuna Jr. to ground out to second and end the inning. Neither team mounted much of an attack, with Yamamoto finishing out another spectacular seven-inning start with just one run allowed and 10 strikeouts. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER That set up yet another drama-filled bottom of the 9th inning, with Dodgers manager Dave Roberts making a gutsy, and controversial, choice to close it out. After using Tanner Scott in the 8th against 9-1-2, and eventually 3, Roberts turned to ... Edwin Diaz for the final three outs. Diaz finished the regular season with an 8.68 ERA in 21 games, blew four saves in 11 opportunities, and wasn't guaranteed a spot on the postseason roster. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD Immediately, it looked like the move would backfire. Diaz gave up a ringing lead-off double to Ozzie Albies, putting the tying run at the plate for Michael Harris, Dubon, and pinch hitter Mike Yastrzemski. But Diaz got out of it, getting Harris to ground out, Dubon flew out in foul territory without allowing the run to score, and Yastrzemski hit a soft grounder to short to end it. Another close, exciting playoff game, in a postseason filled with them. For the Dodgers, beating Sale gives them a tremendous advantage to close out the series. Tyler Mahle starts game four on Wednesday night, and while he's been outstanding since the trade deadline, his career track record is less impressive. LA now knows the worst case scenario is Tyler Glasnow for game four, and Tarik Skubal for game five. The Braves, though, can point to their offense as a place for improvement. Baldwin, Acuna, and Olson haven't done much in the series, with Harris providing most of the offense. And if they can extend the series to a decisive game five, Sale will be available again out of the bullpen. But their season is now on the brink, and the Dodgers will likely go all out to avoid a return trip to LA and set up their rotation for the NLCS. As always, must-see TV.

articles.title: New Alex Cora Rumors Reveal Managerial Decision for 2027 MLB Season Amid Phillies Buzz
articles.summary: Alex Cora reportedly won't be the next manager of the Philadelphia Phillies.
articles.body:
Alex Cora reportedly won't be the next manager of the Philadelphia Phillies.

According to USA Today's Bob Nightengale , Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski spoke to Cora about becoming the team's new manager. Cora revealed that he's taking the 2027 season off, though.

He was previously offered Philadelphia's manager role in April and declined it to spend the rest of the summer with his family, per Nightengale.

Cora opened the 2026 season as manager of the Boston Red Sox, but was fired after the team started with a disappointing 10-17 record.

The Phillies also made an early manager change during their 2026 campaign, parting ways with Rob Thomson after a 9-13 start to the year.

Don Mattingly served as Philadelphia's interim manager for the remainder of the season, as the team finished with an 88-74 record and made a playoff appearance. The Phillies were ultimately eliminated from the postseason by the Atlanta Braves during their National League Wild Card Series matchup.

Mattingly has expressed interest in remaining Philadelphia's manager beyond the 2026 season, although the team has yet to make a decision regarding his future.

The Phillies' interest in Cora is understandable, as Dombrowski previously spent time with him in Boston from 2018-19.

Cora compiled a 620-541 overall record with the Red Sox, helping them make four postseason appearances in his first seven years as a member of the club. This included a 2018 campaign in which Boston captured its ninth World Series title.

articles.title: Closer Mason Miller hits paternity list 45 minutes before the Padres' season is on the line
articles.summary: Mason Miller lands on MLB's paternity list before a win-or-go-home Game 3, leaving the Padres without their top reliever in an elimination game.
articles.body: San Diego Padres All-Star reliever Mason Miller will miss an elimination game against the Milwaukee Brewers after being placed on Major League Baseball’s paternity list ahead of Game 3 of the National League Division Series. Miller couldn't have picked a worse time to step away, leaving San Diego without its top bullpen weapon right before a win-or-go-home Game 3. The team placed him on the paternity list 45 minutes before the start of the game. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under MLB’s postseason paternity rules, Miller is allowed up to three days off. The Pads plugged that hole by putting veteran lefty Wandy Peralta on the active roster. If San Diego somehow manages to keep its season alive, Miller gets his spot back whenever he returns. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Baseball fans couldn't help but draw comparisons to Yankees starter Max Fried, who finds himself in the exact same boat. Fried is slated to pitch a crucial Game 3 with his girlfriend due any day, but he publicly confirmed he isn't skipping his start for anything. Seeing Fried post up for his team while Miller sits out an elimination game brought the debate over playoff priorities right to the forefront. Making matters worse, Miller’s last act on Sunday was a total disappointment. Trusted to secure a six-out save in Game 2, he unravelled with two outs and two strikes in the ninth, giving up a walk-off single to Jackson Chourio. Congratulations are in order for the new dad, but if San Diego gets eliminated, fans won't be in much of a mood to celebrate. articles.title: Yamamoto dominant again as Dodgers ride homers from Hernández, Freeman to 3-1 win over Braves
articles.summary: Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed only four hits, helping the Los Angeles win 3-1 over Atlanta and take a 2-1 lead in the NL Division Series.
articles.body: ATLANTA — Yoshinobu Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series. Yamamoto dominated the much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Yamamoto, the MVP of the 2025 World Series, permitted only four hits with one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts. His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for the Japanese right-hander. The Dodgers can win the best-of-five series and take another step in their attempt to become the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series titles by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4. The Braves hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth. Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Edwin Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II’s groundout. Díaz stranded the runner when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts. Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn’t be denied an inning later. Hernández’s homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta. Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order. With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher’s interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a fly ball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta’s fourth pitcher. Baldwin’s bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta’s only run. Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain. Tanner Scott added two strikeouts in a scoreless eighth for Los Angeles. Up next Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.

articles.title: Dodgers grind down Chris Sale as Braves' offensive woes continue in NLDS Game 3 loss
articles.summary: Any one of the Braves' big hitters could've tied this game with a timely swing. The problem is they didn't.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — In the middle of every fifth inning at home, the Braves roll out a promotion in which a fan races "The Freeze," a sprinter in an ice-blue bodysuit. The fan gets a head start to run around the perimeter of the outfield, but soon enough, the Freeze starts hunting. On Tuesday, a fan in a Ronald Acuña Jr. jersey outran The Freeze for a surprisingly long distance … but eventually face-planted on the warning-track dirt just as The Freeze cruised past him to victory.

As metaphors for the Braves' 3-1 NLDS Game 3 loss to the Dodgers go, it was pretty on the nose. With everything set up in its favor — a split on the road, ace on the hill, full home stadium on a perfect, 74-degree night — Atlanta slipped just once and was lost.

Diagnosing what went wrong in this game for the Braves, who now face elimination on Wednesday, isn't hard. Starter Chris Sale made, by his estimation, two bad pitches, both of which ended up in the Truist Park seats. The Braves' key hitters weren't able to match the Dodgers' fireworks, perpetuating a run of ice-cold hitting that's now threatening to end their season.

"We've just got to get some key hits in key moments and get guys comfortable. It's as simple as that," Austin Riley said after the game in a quiet Braves locker room. "We had some opportunities tonight and just didn't get it done."

Sale, fresh off a dominant bookend performance in the wild-card series victory over Philadelphia, took the mound on full rest on Tuesday. And while he struck out seven over five innings, he had to go deep into the count on virtually every batter.

"They did a nice job of really grinding the at-bats and passing the baton," Braves manager Walt Weiss said postgame. "He had to work hard. He had to work hard to get the outs that he got."

You see that many pitches, and you start to pick out some favorites, and by the fourth inning, the Dodgers did exactly that. Kiké Hernández rifled a 92-mph inside changeup 406 feet, scoring Andy Pages. Two batters later, Freddie Freeman turned on an inside sinker to put the score at 3-0 — a Dodgers run total that would hold up the rest of the game.

"One bad inning ruined the whole game," Sale said. "Yanked a changeup to Kiké. We all know what he can do in October when the lights are bright. Actually made a pretty good pitch to Freddie, but he was either looking for it or saw it out of the hand."

One inning later, with 95 pitches in the books, Sale was cashed. "Getting Chris Sale out of the game after five innings," Freeman said later, "is a huge win no matter what the score is."

The Braves probably could've weathered a subpar — by Sale's standards — outing from their ace. But the vibes were off all game for Atlanta, both in the field and in the stands. The fans made the wrong choice in the cap shuffle game. The stadium PA tried to fire up the fans with "make some noise!" blasts, which really shouldn't be necessary in October. And, of course, there was the guy in the Acuña jersey walking away from his race against The Freeze with nothing but a mouthful of dirt.

That guy was only mirroring the struggles of the real Acuña, who's now 3-for-21 — with three singles — in this postseason. In Game 3, he had his moment teed up — the bottom of the fifth, two men on, down 3-1 — but Acuña could only ground out, killing the Braves' best scoring chance of the night.

An Ozzie Albies double to start the ninth gave the Braves one last chance at late heroics, with the tying run at the plate and no outs. But three batters later, Atlanta was done. And the questions about the Braves' offensive whimpering only gained strength.

Afterward, Weiss pushed back on the idea that Acuña, Drake Baldwin (3-for-23, six strikeouts this postseason) and Matt Olson (4-for-23, 1 homer, 9 strikeouts) are mired in unbreakable slumps.

"Those guys have been our aircraft carriers all year," he said. "Every time one of those guys steps in the box, I think something good is going to happen. Those guys, they're always one at-bat away from changing a game."

He's right. The Dodgers are relentless, yes, but also beatable. Any one of the Braves' big hitters could have tied this game — or won it — with a timely swing. The problem is they didn't, and now there aren't that many at-bats left for the Braves to salvage their season.

"We've had our back against the wall before," Sale said. "We're a resilient group. We have confidence in ourselves and each other. So, yeah, we'll take this one off the chin and show up [Wednesday] ready to win a game."

Braves fans (and the tight surrounding buildings) can make Truist Park one of the loudest in baseball, but the fans are also a trailing indicator of the team's performance; they need to see some results before they truly commit to cheering. (One of the loudest spontaneous reactions of the night: the boos for Freeman, a former hometown hero . Nothing but love between Freddie and the Atlanta fans, but this is October.)

With grinding patience, Los Angeles was able to take Sale out of the game and the fight out of the crowd on Tuesday, and neither the Braves nor their fans could get up off the deck. Now everyone in a Braves uniform — both on the field and in the stands — will have one more chance to extend this season, one more chance to avoid an offseason of second-guessing and what-could-have-been.

articles.title: Yoshinobu Yamamoto adds to his already sterling postseason résumé, puts the Dodgers back in control in NLDS Game 3: 'He's just not afraid'
articles.summary: Yamamoto delivered 7 innings of 1-run ball as the Dodgers took a 2-1 series lead in Atlanta.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — Will Smith couldn't make out exactly what Yoshinobu Yamamoto was saying.

Perhaps it was the language barrier. The Dodgers had already made a mound visit in the fifth inning, meaning interpreter Will Ireton could not reemerge from the dugout. And so, only Smith and third baseman Kiké Hernández, a close confidant of Yamamoto's, joined the all-world hurler on the hill.

Or maybe Yamamoto was drowned out by the Truist Park crowd, rising, chanting, chopping, glad to finally be in the presence of something worth cheering for.

Because after four innings of calm dominance, Yamamoto, October's sharpest buzzsaw, looked to be on the ropes in NLDS Game 3 .

Atlanta's offense, down 3-0 in the fifth, had juiced the bases with one out. As Yamamoto, Smith and Hernández congregated on the mound, Drake Baldwin, leadoff hitter and All-Star, lurked ominously in the left-handed batter's box. Darude's "Sandstorm" jumped from the ballpark speakers. A moment, the kind that makes playoff baseball a special beast, was building.

The Braves had found themselves in possession of something rare, something precious, something worth seizing: a postseason opportunity against one of the greats. For the first time all season, Yamamoto was unmoored enough to require two mound visits in the same inning.

But Hernández, as he has been so often for the Dodgers over the years, was in the right place at the right time.

"[I went to the mound] because of the relationship with Yoshi and what we've gone through together," Hernández told Yahoo Sports after Los Angeles' 3-1 win on Tuesday . "I'm glad I was there."

The L.A. stalwart and cult hero, whose fourth-inning, two-run blast (his 17th career postseason homer) had gotten the scoring started, understood what Yamamoto was trying to convey and knew how to communicate it to Smith.

"I was able to translate because of my good Japanese," he added in jest.

"That was an encouraging moment," Yamamoto acknowledged afterward. "He told me just be yourself, even though that was a little bit like a dirty word."

The Braves, after failing to take advantage, likely uttered a cuss or two themselves.

Baldwin grounded out meekly to first, driving in Atlanta's first run in the process. That brought the slumping Ronald Acuña Jr. to the dish with the chance for a signature October highlight. Instead, the 2023 NL MVP bounced an inning-ending, rally-burning, game-killing, potentially season-altering grounder to second baseman Miguel Rojas. The threat was quelled, the window was closed. The reigning World Series MVP, and his three-peat-seeking ballclub, were back in control.

Yamamoto set down the next six hitters he faced, breezily tossing up zeros in the sixth and seventh frames before giving way to Los Angeles' bullpen. In all, it was yet another sensational October outing by the diminutive right-hander: 7 innings, 1 run, 10 strikeouts.

"Wow. What a performance," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts gushed postgame. "... He just has a way to just make pitches, calm his heartbeat."

So much of the conversation entering Tuesday's crucial contest centered on Braves ace Chris Sale, who, after Atlanta's surprise Game 2 victory , had a chance to push the Dodgers to the brink. But the Dodgers ground Sale down in the early going , working up his pitch count and setting the stage for Hernández's big swing in the fourth. Sale was done after five.

Yamamoto, on the other hand, went seven innings in a playoff game for the third time since he came over from Japan ahead of 2024. The only other player to accomplish that in the same span? Dodgers Game 1 starter Tarik Skubal.

"He's just not afraid," catcher Will Smith said of Yamamoto.

And while Yamamoto's secured eternal-hero status with that Game 7, no-rest, World Series relief appearance for the ages, the totality of his postseason résumé is similarly impressive, historic, awe-inspiring.

After Tuesday's gem, Yamamoto holds the second-lowest postseason career ERA in MLB history among pitchers with at least 10 postseason starts. The only name ahead of him, San Francisco Giants icon Madison Bumgarner, is well within reach, with a 2.11 to Yamamoto's 2.14. And the Dodgers' ace, almost certainly, should have many, many more chances to shrink that number. He's still just 28 years old, and Los Angeles is in the playoffs every year.

The legend is already large, yet the legend is still building.

Somehow, the same can be said for Hernández, who at 35 years old, was not guaranteed to be part of this year's Dodgers story. After playing a key role in last year's epic Game 7 alongside Yamamoto, Hernández hit the free-agent market. A return to L.A. was far from certain. He hadn't been a league-average hitter since the 2021 season. Age and injuries were starting to pile up.

Then he re-signed with the Dodgers late in the offseason, after pitchers and catchers had reported, but appeared in just 41 games. His health and his place on this October roster were never a given.

Yet in some ways, this was also inevitable.

Amidst Los Angeles' financial might and player development prowess and institutional grandeur, Hernández represents a more human side of this juggernaut. If Yamamoto, alongside Shohei Ohtani, is a cornerstone of this glorious Dodgers run and all it represents, Hernández is an appreciated connection to a bygone era, a holdover with a clutch gene.

This mercurial goofball has been a fundamental part of this organization's DNA for the better part of the past decade. He is a flawed ballplayer, in a year-over-year decline. He is also indispensable. After not playing in the first two games of this series, Hérnandez delivered the biggest swing of its third. And nobody was particularly surprised. All those experiences in big moments allow Hernández to be thoroughly unperturbed by the scale of it all. None of this feels big to him anymore, even if it still does to the rest of us.

"I don't know how much it means," Hernández responded to a reporter's question about what the home run meant to him. "But it feels good."

So do the Dodgers, back where they believe they belong, with a 2-1 series lead, thanks to these two dissimilar postseason pillars.

articles.title: Padres Beat Brewers to Avoid Elimination, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: The San Diego Padres aren't done yet.
articles.body:
San Diego defeated the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 in Tuesday's Game 3 of their National League Division series at Petco Park. Milwaukee still leads the series 2-1, but the Padres now have momentum thanks to timely hitting and clutch pitching.

Jake Cronenworth launched a homer, Manny Machado and Fernando Tatis Jr. each notched an RBI, and the shorthanded bullpen got the job done to preserve the season.

A return home was an opportunity for the Padres to put two shocking losses behind them and work toward a potential comeback. It seemed as if they were going to take the lead in the ninth inning of Game 1 when Ty France launched a deep fly ball with a man on base that may have cleared the fence, but it hit the roof and fell into Jackson Chourio's glove for an out.

As if that wasn't difficult enough, San Diego had the lead in the bottom of the ninth in Game 2 just for star closer Mason Miller to blow a save.

A quick start to move on seemed paramount, and the home team got just that thanks to small ball in the third inning. Samad Taylor singled, stole a base, advanced on a bunt and scored on Tatis' RBI ground out before Jackson Merrill singled, stole a base and scored on Machado's RBI single.

Milwaukee chased Padres starter Nick Pivetta from the game after 4.1 innings with William Contreras cutting the deficit in half with a solo homer and Chourio tying it with a sacrifice fly that featured aggressive base running from Cooper Pratt.

With Brewers starter Dustin May already unable to record an out past the third, it was a bullpen game the rest of the way. Bullpen games typically favor the Padres on paper, but they were without Miller because he was placed on the paternity list.

Unlike the first two games, it was San Diego that responded in the pressure-packed moments Tuesday.

Cronenworth broke the tie with a solo homer in the fifth, while Xander Bogaerts provided some breathing room when he singled, advanced on a wild pitch and scored on a throwing error from Pratt in the sixth.

Still, putting away the Brewers is never easy. Bradgley Rodriguez escaped with runners on second and third in the sixth, but he gave up an RBI single to Christian Yelich in the seventh before striking out Garrett Mitchell to avoid more damage.

With Miller unavailable and questions looming about Adrian Morejon's availability, San Diego turned to Game 2 starter Michael King in a stunning development.

All he did was pitch a scoreless eighth and remain in the game to close the door in the ninth by inducing a double play from Yelich.

articles.title: Padres closer Mason Miller misses Game 3 win over Brewers after being added to paternity list
articles.summary: Mason Miller was tied for third in MLB in saves this year with 38.
articles.body:
The San Diego Padres found a way to extend their season without All-Star closer Mason Miller.

The Padres climbed back into the NLDS and beat the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 on Tuesday at Petco Park. That gave them their first win in the series and forced Game 4 on Wednesday.

And they did it all without their star closer.

MLB approved a roster change for San Diego on Tuesday afternoon, as Miller landed on the postseason paternity list. Miller's wife, who was due to give birth to the couple's first child later this month, went into labor Tuesday afternoon. As a result, the All-Star was not available for Game 3. The Padres replaced him with reliever Wandy Peralta.

The MLB playoffs come with specific roster rules. A team must submit a roster for each series. If a player is replaced during a series due to injury, he must miss that series and , if the team advances, the following series.

But Miller was added to the postseason paternity list, and there are different rules for that. He can miss a minimum of one day and a maximum of three. When he returns, he can replace Peralta without being forced to sit out another series.

Miller is one of baseball's best closers. He had a career-high 38 saves this season in 66 appearances and finished with a 1.67 ERA.

The 35-year-old Peralta gives the Padres an extra lefty out of the bullpen. He made 65 appearances this season and went 3-3 with a 3.61 ERA.

San Diego is still on the brink of elimination in the best-of-five series. Games 1 and 2 both came down to the wire, with the Brew Crew winning each by one run.

Miller blew the save in Game 2 , when Jackson Chourio laced a walk-off single to center that drove in both Sal Frelick and Christian Yelich, giving Milwaukee a 4-3 victory.

After the Padres' win at home on Tuesday, the series continues with Game 4 on Wednesday in San Diego. Miller is eligible to return for that contest. Whether he'll be ready to do so remains to be seen.

articles.title: Padres hold off Brewers in must-win Game 3 to survive elimination and force Game 4 at Petco Park
articles.summary: Michael King stranded the tying run in the ninth as the San Diego Padres staved off elimination with a 4-3 NLDS Game 3 win over the Brewers.
articles.body: The first two games of the National League Division Series matchup between the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers have been playoff baseball at its best. Drama, late-inning heroics, the American Family Field roof suddenly coming into play, and series-changing moments between two of the best players in Major League Baseball. Game one saw William Contreras launch a go-ahead homer in the 7th inning, while Ty France tried to hit a go-ahead one in the top of the ninth, only to be thwarted by the roof support system in Milwaukee. The Brewers held on to win that game, 3-2, setting up a must-win for the Padres in game two. Michael King out-dueled Logan Henderson, and the Padres' talented bullpen mostly held Milwaukee's lineup at bay ... until the bottom of the ninth inning. CLOSER MASON MILLER HITS PATERNITY LIST 45 MINUTES BEFORE THE PADRES' SEASON IS ON THE LINE All-world closer Mason Miller, starting his second inning of work, suddenly couldn't find the plate. After three walks in the inning, star outfielder Jackson Chourio crushed a line-drive single to center field, walking off the Padres and giving the Brewers a commanding 2-0 series lead with the series shifting to Petco Park. With Miller pushed to 40 pitches on Sunday, his availability for Tuesday's must-win matchup was already in question. But some stunning pregame news, that he'd be placed on the paternity list and unavailable, removed any doubt. Fortunately for San Diego, they had Nick Pivetta starting against Dustin May, seemingly providing a clear matchup advantage. Through the early part of the game, that's exactly how it played out. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Pivetta used some spectacular defense from Jackson Merrill to work a scoreless first inning, with the young center fielder making a fantastic catch to rob Chourio of a double. While Dustin May got through the first few innings unscathed, the third quickly unraveled. Samad Taylor singled and stole second, with Jake Cronenworth bunting him to third. Fernando Tatis Jr. hit a run-scoring grounder to make it 1-0, followed by Merrill lacing a single to center. He too stole second, and Manny Machado, struggling through the first two games, finally came through and drove in the second run to send the San Diego crowd into a frenzy. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER In the top of the fourth, Milwaukee struck back. William Contreras, coming off a down year by his standards, delivered again, launching a mammoth homer to left field off Pivetta. And he took his sweet time admiring it, adding some celebrations while rounding the bases. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD That made it 2-1, and when the Padres worked a lead off walk in the bottom of the fourth, Brewers manager Pat Murphy didn't hesitate, removing May from the game and going to the strong Milwaukee bullpen. Milwaukee didn't stay down for long. In the top of the fifth, Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick set the table with back-to-back singles, allowing Jackson Chourio to knot the game at 2-2 with a sacrifice fly to center. But Jake Cronenworth wasn't having it. In the bottom of the fifth, Cronenworth launched a majestic solo shot to right field off Antonio Senzatela, restoring San Diego's lead at 3-2 and sending Petco Park into a frenzy. The Padres tacked on a crucial insurance run in the sixth when Xander Bogaerts came home on a Cooper Pratt throwing error to push the lead to 4-2. Milwaukee battled back in the eighth, scratching across another run off Bradgley Rodríguez to cut the deficit to 4-3. But Padres manager Craig Stammen turned to starter-turned-reliever Michael King to finish the job. King tossed two gritty innings out of the bullpen, stranding the tying run in the ninth to secure the 4-3 victory. With the 4-3 win, San Diego fended off the sweep, cut Milwaukee’s NLDS lead to 2-1, and set up a massive Game 4 at Petco Park. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE This entire series has been a showcase of top-tier baseball; elite pitching, powerful bullpens, and stars coming through in big moments. If this doesn't go five games, it'll be a missed opportunity for neutral fans who enjoy the drama of playoff baseball. Though Milwaukee is certainly hoping it doesn't.

articles.title: Padres avoid elimination after 4-3 win over Brewers in NLDS Game 3
articles.summary: Jake Cronenworth hit a tiebreaking homer, Game 2 starter Michael King pitched the final two innings on one day of rest and the San Diego Padres avoided playoff elimination with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of their NL Division Series on Tuesday night.
articles.body: SAN DIEGO — Jake Cronenworth hit a tiebreaking homer, Game 2 starter Michael King pitched the final two innings on one day of rest and the San Diego Padres avoided playoff elimination with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of their NL Division Series on Tuesday night. Xander Bogaerts turned a game-ending double play at shortstop for the Padres, who trimmed Milwaukee’s lead in the best-of-five series to 2-1 with a tense, back-and-forth victory over the MLB-best Brewers. Game 4 is Wednesday night at Petco Park. If necessary, Game 5 will be back in Milwaukee on Friday. Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado drove in early runs for the Padres, but their bullpen didn’t have star closer Mason Miller, who went on the paternity list about 45 minutes before the first pitch. King stepped up after pitching five innings just two days ago and finished it off — but only after a thrilling ninth. The right-hander retired four of his first five batters, but William Contreras and Brice Turang drew one-out walks in the ninth. Christian Yelich then cracked a 107 mph line drive up the middle, where Bogaerts went down to his knees to field it on a short hop and scampered to touch second base before throwing out Yelich at first to end it. King earned his first save since 2023, his first in the postseason and his first for the Padres. Contreras homered and had three hits for the Brewers, who lost their 12th consecutive postseason road game dating to the 2018 National League Championship Series. Yelich even got his first playoff RBI since 2018 with a seventh-inning single, but Milwaukee fell behind early and never led, leaving 11 runners on base. Padres back on track The Padres had won 19 of 22 and swept the Cubs out of the Wild Card Series before losing two straight heartbreakers in Milwaukee last weekend, but they are fighting to stay with the majors’ best regular-season team. The clubs have played three consecutive one-run games in this NLDS, all decided by late-game execution — and this time, the Padres came through. They were also bailed out by King, largely a reliever early in his major league career with the Yankees. This game was just his third relief appearance in three seasons with San Diego — and according to OptaStats, he is the first pitcher to start a postseason game and then earn a two-inning save within the next two days since saves became an official statistic in 1969. Back-and-forth game Neither starter excelled on a tense, uncommonly hot October night in downtown San Diego. Nick Pivetta yielded two runs and five hits while pitching into the fifth for the Padres, and Dustin May got pulled abruptly with a 1-0 count on Bogaerts and a runner on in the fourth. Samad Taylor and Jackson Merrill put San Diego ahead in the third when both singled, stole second and scored. Contreras answered with his second homer of the series, adding a theatrical trot around the bases. Cooper Pratt tied it right after Pivetta’s exit when Dustin Harris couldn’t throw him out on Jackson Chourio’s 242-foot sacrifice fly. It was the fifth RBI of the series for the 22-year-old Chourio and his 16th in 15 career postseason games, already tying Ryan Braun for the franchise record. Cronenworth lined JoJo Romero’s first pitch of the fifth over the wall in right for only his second hit of the postseason. Bogaerts then singled in the sixth, advanced on a wild pitch and scored when Pratt bounced his throw from shortstop for an error after Miguel Andujar’s broken bat came flying toward him along with the grounder. San Diego’s outfield couldn’t get to Turang’s bloop single with two outs in the seventh, and Yelich singled home Contreras for his first playoff RBI since he homered in Game 7 of the 2018 NLCS against the Dodgers — a span of 87 plate appearances over 19 games. Up next Neither team had announced its Game 4 starter.
